screens.title: Dependency Injection & Inversion of Control
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection matter for clean code. IoC is the principle that the system’s control flow is inverted so that components receive behavior from an external orchestrator rather than creating it themselves. Dependency Injection is a concrete technique to apply IoC: rather than instantiating required collaborators inside a class, you supply them from the outside. This reduces coupling, makes classes easier to test with mocks or stubs, and helps you swap implementations for different environments. You'll see concrete C# examples showing an interface-based repository and two implementations, and a hands-on Python refactor to practice constructor injection. We will also compare constructor, setter, and interface injection, and point out common smells like over-injecting dependencies or creating a “God object.” By the end, you should be able to choose an injection strategy, refactor a tightly coupled class, and know when an IoC container helps manage composition. Think of this chapter as a practical toolkit for producing maintainable, testable modules.

screens.title: Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection — Definitions
screens.narratorSegment: Inversion of Control is a design principle that flips who controls how components interact. Instead of your class creating and orchestrating its collaborators, an external system or composition root supplies those collaborators. Dependency Injection is a specific way to realize IoC: a class declares what it needs and receives those dependencies from the outside. This separation of concerns matters because creation and composition are different responsibilities than business logic. When a class stops creating its dependencies, it focuses on behavior, and composition can be changed without touching its code. A concrete example: a UserService should not instantiate a S Q L repository directly. If UserService receives an IUserRepository instead, you can swap in an in-memory repository for tests, or a different database implementation for another environment. A common misconception is to conflate IoC with a specific framework; IoC is a principle, DI is a pattern, and containers are tools that help wire them up. Key takeaway: think of composition as a separate job from behavior — that leads to easier testing, swapping, and adherence to SOLID principles. Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection — Definitions means ioc inverts control; di supplies dependencies so classes remain focused on behavior.. In practical terms, what ioc and di mean and why that distinction matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: IoC inverts control; DI supplies dependencies so classes remain focused on behavior.

content.html:
Core Concept
Inversion of Control
IoC separates composition from behavior. A component stops creating its collaborators and instead expects them to be provided. This makes the component independent from the concrete creation process.
Why it matters
Separating composition reduces coupling and allows different environments or tests to supply alternate implementations.
Concrete example
A UserService receives an IUserRepository. Tests can pass InMemoryUserRepository instead of a SQL implementation to isolate logic from storage.
Common misconception
IoC is not the same as using a container. You can apply IoC by manual composition without any framework.
Definition
Dependency Injection
DI is a pattern to implement IoC. A class declares requirements and accepts collaborators via constructor, setter, or an injection method. The important effect is that the class has no responsibility for creating its dependencies.
Forms of DI
Constructor injection ensures required dependencies are present. Setter injection suits optional dependencies. Interface injection uses a contract method to accept dependencies.
Key takeaway
When classes stop creating collaborators they become easier to test, change, and reason about.

screens.title: Direct Instantiation vs Injected Dependencies
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare two common approaches. In direct instantiation, a class creates its own collaborators with new or direct construction. This couples the class to a specific implementation and mixes composition with behavior. As a result, swapping implementations or writing isolated unit tests requires modifying the class or using heavy test harnesses. In contrast, injected dependencies are passed into the class, usually via constructor parameters or setters. The class depends only on an interface, not a concrete type, so you can replace the implementation for testing or different environments without changing the class itself. For example, a UserService that constructs SqlUserRepository cannot be tested without a database; a UserService that accepts an IUserRepository can be tested with an InMemoryUserRepository. A typical misconception is that DI always requires a container; it does not. Manual wiring is a valid first step. Key takeaway: injection decouples creation from behavior, enabling easier testing and evolution. Direct Instantiation vs Injected Dependencies means direct creation ties behavior to implementation. injection decouples them so code is flexible and testable.. In practical terms, how control and coupling differ in each approach. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison insight
keyIdea.text: Direct creation ties behavior to implementation. Injection decouples them so code is flexible and testable.

content.html:
Comparison
Direct Instantiation
Class creates its own collaborator. This causes tight coupling and hard-to-test code.
Example
UserService calls new SqlUserRepository() internally and performs persistence directly.
Drawback
Tests require a database or complex fakes; swapping implementations requires code changes.
Comparison
Injected Dependency
Class receives an interface implementation from outside and focuses on behavior.
Example
UserService constructor accepts IUserRepository; the composition root provides SqlUserRepository or InMemoryUserRepository.
Benefit
Tests can pass a simple in-memory repository; implementations can be swapped without touching business code.
Key Takeaway
Prefer injection for collaborators that influence behavior and environment. Use direct instantiation only for pure value objects or simple, internal helpers.

screens.title: C# Example — IUserRepository and UserService
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the C# example from the chapter to see constructor injection in action. The pattern starts with an interface that defines the contract, for example IUserRepository with GetUserById and SaveUser. Because UserService depends on the interface only, the composition root can pass whichever implementation is appropriate. keyIdea.title: Constructor Injection
keyIdea.text: Provide dependencies through the constructor so the object is always initialized with required collaborators.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
IUserRepository and implementations
The code below defines the interface, two implementations, and a service that receives an IUserRepository via constructor injection.
// Define the contract for user data access
public interface IUserRepository
{
  User GetUserById(int id);
  void SaveUser(User user);
}

// SQL implementation
public class SqlUserRepository : IUserRepository
{
  private readonly string _connectionString;
  public SqlUserRepository(string connectionString)
  {
    _connectionString = connectionString;
  }
  public User GetUserById(int id)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Fetching user {id} from SQL DB using {_connectionString}");
    return new User { Id = id, Name = $"UserFromSql{id}" };
  }
  public void SaveUser(User user)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Saving user {user.Id} to SQL DB using {_connectionString}");
  }
}

// In-memory implementation for testing
public class InMemoryUserRepository : IUserRepository
{
  private readonly Dictionary _users = new Dictionary();
  public User GetUserById(int id)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Fetching user {id} from In-Memory DB");
    return _users.TryGetValue(id, out var user) ? user : null;
  }
  public void SaveUser(User user)
  {
    Console.WriteLine($"Saving user {user.Id} to In-Memory DB");
    _users[user.Id] = user;
  }
}

// UserService depends on IUserRepository
public class UserService
{
  private readonly IUserRepository _userRepository;
  public UserService(IUserRepository userRepository)
  {
    _userRepository = userRepository ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(userRepository));
  }
  public User GetUserDetails(int userId)
  {
    return _userRepository.GetUserById(userId);
  }
}
Explanation
  • IUserRepository defines the contract used by UserService.
  • SqlUserRepository and InMemoryUserRepository implement the same contract and can be swapped.
  • UserService receives the dependency through its constructor and remains implementation-agnostic.
Concrete example
Create SqlUserRepository in production and InMemoryUserRepository for tests; pass each into UserService without changing its logic.
Check
If a constructor has many dependencies, consider splitting responsibilities; long constructors are a smell.

screens.title: Constructor Injection — What to do and why
screens.narratorSegment: Constructor injection is the recommended default for required dependencies because it guarantees an object is created in a valid state. Follow a simple process: first identify required collaborators that the class cannot function without. Second, add constructor parameters typed to interfaces or abstract contracts rather than concrete classes. Third, assign those parameters to readonly fields so behavior can rely on stable collaborators. Fourth, perform manual wiring in a composition root or let a container resolve the graph. Finally, write tests that pass lightweight fakes or in-memory implementations to exercise class logic without external resources. A practical example: if ReportGenerator always needs an IDataReader, require it in the constructor; this makes tests deterministic by passing a fake IDataReader. A common misconception is that constructor injection prevents optional dependencies; for optional collaborators prefer setter injection or a small adapter to keep required dependencies clear. The key takeaway: constructor injection enforces valid initialization and makes dependencies explicit, improving readability and safety. Constructor Injection — What to do and why means use constructor injection for required collaborators to ensure consistent, testable initialization.. In practical terms, a step-by-step process for using constructor injection safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Constructor pattern
keyIdea.text: Use constructor injection for required collaborators to ensure consistent, testable initialization.

content.html:
Process Flow
Constructor Injection — Steps
1. Identify
List required collaborators the class cannot run without.
2. Declare
Add constructor parameters typed to interfaces, not concrete classes.
3. Assign
Store dependencies in readonly fields so behavior relies on stable collaborators.
4. Wire
Compose objects in a composition root or use a container to resolve them.
5. Test
Pass fakes or in-memory implementations to test behavior without external systems.
Example
ReportGenerator requires IDataReader in constructor. Tests pass a FakeDataReader to validate report logic without I/O.
Pitfall
If constructors grow too large, the class likely violates SRP; split responsibilities first.
Key Takeaway
Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and enforces valid object creation.

screens.title: Setter and Interface Injection — Options and Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Setter injection and interface injection exist for cases where constructor injection is inconvenient. Setter injection exposes a public property or method so you can assign a dependency after object construction. This is useful for optional collaborators or for scenarios where a dependency must be set later in the lifecycle. However, setter injection can leave objects in an invalid or partially-initialized state if callers forget to set the property. Interface injection requires the dependent class to implement an interface that provides an injection method; the injector calls that method to supply the dependency. This pattern is less common in modern codebases but can be useful when frameworks or libraries expect a particular injection contract. A concrete caution: use setter injection for genuinely optional capabilities, and keep required collaborators in the constructor. If you see many setters for dependencies, reconsider the design — the class might be taking on too many responsibilities. Always balance flexibility with clear initialization guarantees. In practical terms, when optional or late-bound dependencies make sense. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Optional injection
keyIdea.text: Setter and interface injection allow later assignment but can create invalid states; prefer them for optional dependencies only.

content.html:
Definition
Setter Injection
Provide dependencies via public properties or setter methods after construction. Useful for optional features or late binding.
When to use
Optional logging, telemetry, or optional extensions that are not required for core behavior.
Risk
Objects can be in an invalid state if setters are not called. Validate state where necessary.
Definition
Interface Injection
The dependent class implements an interface that exposes an injection method. The injector calls that method to provide the dependency.
When it appears
Mostly seen in older frameworks or where an explicit injection contract is required.
Trade-off
It couples the dependent class to the injection contract, which can be less flexible than constructor injection.
Key Takeaway
Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies. Use setter or interface injection only for optional or lifecycle-specific needs, and validate state to avoid surprises.

screens.title: IoC Containers — Why and When to Use Them
screens.narratorSegment: IoC containers are tools that automate the manual wiring of object graphs. For small applications, manual composition is clear and simple. As systems grow, manually creating and passing dependencies can become tedious and error-prone. Containers let you register interface-to-implementation mappings and resolve composed objects, often with lifecycle options such as singleton or transient. This makes it easy to switch implementations per environment: register SqlUserRepository in production and InMemoryUserRepository in tests. The container also centralizes configuration and can manage object lifetimes, reducing boilerplate in composition roots. However, containers add complexity and can obscure where dependencies come from if overused. Use containers when your application has many components and wiring logic that you'd rather declare than hand-code. Maintain readability by keeping composition in a small composition root and avoiding container-driven service location inside your business logic. In practical terms, automating composition and lifecycle management in larger apps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Container guidance
keyIdea.text: Use IoC containers to manage registrations and lifecycles in larger systems, but keep composition visible and centralized.

content.html:
Architecture
IoC Container Role
A container automates registration and resolution of dependencies, simplifying composition for larger applications.
Register
Map an interface to a concrete implementation and configure lifecycles.
Resolve
Ask the container for a composed object and let it inject all required dependencies.
Manage lifecycle
Configure whether components are singletons, transient instances, or scoped to a request.

content.html:
Hands-on Refactor
Starter code (tightly coupled)
# order_processor_tightly_coupled.py

class PaymentGateway:
    def process_payment(self, amount):
        print(f"Processing payment of ${amount} via default gateway.")
        return True

class NotificationService:
    def send_email(self, recipient, message):
        print(f"Sending email to {recipient}: {message}")

class OrderProcessor:
    def __init__(self):
        # Tightly coupled dependencies
        self.payment_gateway = PaymentGateway()
        self.notification_service = NotificationService()

    def process_order(self, order_id, amount, customer_email):
        print(f"Processing order {order_id}...")
        if self.payment_gateway.process_payment(amount):
            self.notification_service.send_email(customer_email, f"Your order {order_id} has been processed.")
            print(f"Order {order_id} processed successfully.")
            return True
        else:
            self.notification_service.send_email(customer_email, f"Payment failed for order {order_id}.")
            print(f"Order {order_id} processing failed.")
            return False
Refactored version
Make dependencies constructor-injected and pass mocks in main or tests.
class OrderProcessor:
    def __init__(self, payment_gateway, notification_service):
        self.payment_gateway = payment_gateway
        self.notification_service = notification_service

    def process_order(self, order_id, amount, customer_email):
        print(f"Processing order {order_id}...")
        if self.payment_gateway.process_payment(amount):
            self.notification_service.send_email(customer_email, f"Your order {order_id} has been processed.")
            print(f"Order {order_id} processed successfully.")
            return True
        else:
            self.notification_service.send_email(customer_email, f"Payment failed for order {order_id}.")
            print(f"Order {order_id} processing failed.")
            return False

# Usage: pass in different implementations or mocks when testing
Why this helps
Tests can pass a FakePaymentGateway and a TestNotificationService to observe behavior without side effects.

screens.title: DI Anti-Patterns and Smells
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection is powerful, but it can be misused. One common anti-pattern is over-injecting: injecting every small object, including simple value objects, which adds unnecessary indirection. Another smell is the constructor with ten or more parameters; this usually indicates the class is doing too much and violates the Single Responsibility Principle. Service locator or container-as-a-global is another problematic pattern where code asks a container for dependencies at runtime, hiding the class’s true requirements. Also watch for injecting mutable global-like services that hide state changes and make tests brittle. To detect these issues, look for long constructors, many setter injections, or frequent runtime resolution calls peppered through business logic. Remediation strategies include splitting responsibilities, creating small factories for collections of related collaborators, or grouping related parameters into small value objects. Key takeaway: use DI to simplify composition but avoid patterns that obscure dependencies or create God objects. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common Pitfalls
DI Anti-Patterns
Over-injecting
Injecting trivial value objects or classes that don't need to be mocked adds complexity.
God objects
Constructors with many parameters indicate the class likely violates SRP and should be split.
Service locator
Hiding dependencies by fetching them from a global container makes code harder to reason about and test.
Mutable global services
Shared mutable services injected everywhere can cause unpredictable behavior in tests.
Remediation
Refactor large classes, group related dependencies, and prefer explicit constructor parameters to make dependencies visible and testable.

screens.title: When to Use DI and Choosing a Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding when to use Dependency Injection comes down to trade-offs. Use DI when a component relies on a collaborator whose behavior may vary by environment, when you need to test behavior without external systems, or when multiple implementations are plausible. For core, always-required collaborators prefer constructor injection because it enforces valid initialization. For optional extensions, use setter injection but validate presence when required. Interface injection is rare; use it only if a framework or legacy pattern demands it. Consider an example given in the chapter: a ReportGenerator that needs different data readers. Constructor injection of an IDataReader is the best option because the report generator cannot function without a data source, making the dependency required for the object's lifetime. Containers become valuable when application composition grows complex and manual wiring becomes a maintenance burden. Key takeaway: match the injection style to the dependency’s role — required, optional, or framework-driven. screens.title: Composition Root and Object Graphs
screens.narratorSegment: The composition root is a central place where the application composes its object graph and wires dependencies. Keep composition code separate from business logic: create concrete implementations and pass them into constructors at application startup or in a small composition module. For example, in a console application you might instantiate SqlUserRepository with its connection string, then create a UserService with that repository and pass UserService to the application entry point. In larger apps this logic can be expressed through a container configuration, but the principle remains: keep wiring visible and controlled. A helpful practice is to centralize configuration for different environments — register in-memory implementations for tests and S Q L ones for production. Avoid scattering new calls across the codebase: that hides dependencies and complicates testing. Key takeaway: centralize composition to make dependencies explicit and easier to manage as the system grows. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection matter for clean code. IoC is the principle that the system’s control flow is inverted so that components receive behavior from an external orchestrator rather than creating it themselves. Dependency Injection is a concrete technique to apply IoC: rather than instantiating required collaborators inside a class, you supply them from the outside. This reduces coupling, makes classes easier to test with mocks or stubs, and helps you swap implementations for different environments. You'll see concrete C# examples showing an interface-based repository and two implementations, and a hands-on Python refactor to practice constructor injection. We will also compare constructor, setter, and interface injection, and point out common smells like over-injecting dependencies or creating a “God object.” By the end, you should be able to choose an injection strategy, refactor a tightly coupled class, and know when an IoC container helps manage composition. Think of this chapter as a practical toolkit for producing maintainable, testable modules.

By the end of the first objectives slide you will be able to state and demonstrate core ideas of IoC and DI. First, you will explain Inversion of Control in plain language: components receive control instead of creating it. Second, you will describe Dependency Injection as the pattern that supplies collaborators from the outside. Third, you will explain how DI leads to decoupling and easier testing, and what that looks like in practice when you replace a concrete repository with a mock. Fourth, you will implement constructor, setter, and interface injection in small examples, recognizing the trade-offs each approach introduces. Each objective is framed as a practical skill: explain the principle, write the injection, or test a class with a mocked dependency. These are the foundational abilities that let you confidently refactor tightly coupled code toward clean, maintainable modules.

On this second objectives slide you'll focus on applied outcomes. You will wire a small constructor-injected object graph manually, and then reason about when an IoC container simplifies that wiring in larger systems. You will be able to explain how a container manages component registration and resolves dependencies at composition time, and why lifecycle choices matter. You will also perform a refactor: take a tightly coupled class and convert it to constructor injection, then run the same behavior with a mock to confirm testability. Finally, you will evaluate scenarios and select constructor injection when a dependency is required for an object's lifetime, setter injection when a dependency is optional, and interface injection when a framework expects a specific injection contract. These practical tasks will make DI a useful tool rather than just an abstract idea.

Inversion of Control is a design principle that flips who controls how components interact. Instead of your class creating and orchestrating its collaborators, an external system or composition root supplies those collaborators. Dependency Injection is a specific way to realize IoC: a class declares what it needs and receives those dependencies from the outside. This separation of concerns matters because creation and composition are different responsibilities than business logic. When a class stops creating its dependencies, it focuses on behavior, and composition can be changed without touching its code. A concrete example: a UserService should not instantiate a S Q L repository directly. If UserService receives an IUserRepository instead, you can swap in an in-memory repository for tests, or a different database implementation for another environment. A common misconception is to conflate IoC with a specific framework; IoC is a principle, DI is a pattern, and containers are tools that help wire them up. Key takeaway: think of composition as a separate job from behavior — that leads to easier testing, swapping, and adherence to SOLID principles. Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection — Definitions means ioc inverts control; di supplies dependencies so classes remain focused on behavior.. In practical terms, what ioc and di mean and why that distinction matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's compare two common approaches. In direct instantiation, a class creates its own collaborators with new or direct construction. This couples the class to a specific implementation and mixes composition with behavior. As a result, swapping implementations or writing isolated unit tests requires modifying the class or using heavy test harnesses. In contrast, injected dependencies are passed into the class, usually via constructor parameters or setters. The class depends only on an interface, not a concrete type, so you can replace the implementation for testing or different environments without changing the class itself. For example, a UserService that constructs SqlUserRepository cannot be tested without a database; a UserService that accepts an IUserRepository can be tested with an InMemoryUserRepository. A typical misconception is that DI always requires a container; it does not. Manual wiring is a valid first step. Key takeaway: injection decouples creation from behavior, enabling easier testing and evolution. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll walk through the C# example from the chapter to see constructor injection in action. The pattern starts with an interface that defines the contract, for example IUserRepository with GetUserById and SaveUser. Two concrete implementations illustrate different environments: SqlUserRepository connects to a database using a connection string, while InMemoryUserRepository stores data in memory for tests. UserService declares a constructor parameter of type IUserRepository and assigns it to a private field. Because UserService depends on the interface only, the composition root can pass whichever implementation is appropriate. In practice you might manually wire the S Q L repository in production and an in-memory repository during tests. A common misconception is that constructor injection requires many parameters; if you see a very long constructor, treat it as a sign the class has too many responsibilities. Constructor injection is the recommended default for required dependencies because it guarantees an object is created in a valid state. Follow a simple process: first identify required collaborators that the class cannot function without. Second, add constructor parameters typed to interfaces or abstract contracts rather than concrete classes. Third, assign those parameters to readonly fields so behavior can rely on stable collaborators. Fourth, perform manual wiring in a composition root or let a container resolve the graph. Setter injection and interface injection exist for cases where constructor injection is inconvenient. Setter injection exposes a public property or method so you can assign a dependency after object construction. This is useful for optional collaborators or for scenarios where a dependency must be set later in the lifecycle. However, setter injection can leave objects in an invalid or partially-initialized state if callers forget to set the property. Interface injection requires the dependent class to implement an interface that provides an injection method; the injector calls that method to supply the dependency. This pattern is less common in modern codebases but can be useful when frameworks or libraries expect a particular injection contract. This makes it easy to switch implementations per environment: register SqlUserRepository in production and InMemoryUserRepository in tests. The container also centralizes configuration and can manage object lifetimes, reducing boilerplate in composition roots. However, containers add complexity and can obscure where dependencies come from if overused. Use containers when your application has many components and wiring logic that you'd rather declare than hand-code. Maintain readability by keeping composition in a small composition root and avoiding container-driven service location inside your business logic. Dependency Injection is powerful, but it can be misused. One common anti-pattern is over-injecting: injecting every small object, including simple value objects, which adds unnecessary indirection. Another smell is the constructor with ten or more parameters; this usually indicates the class is doing too much and violates the Single Responsibility Principle. Service locator or container-as-a-global is another problematic pattern where code asks a container for dependencies at runtime, hiding the class’s true requirements. Also watch for injecting mutable global-like services that hide state changes and make tests brittle. To detect these issues, look for long constructors, many setter injections, or frequent runtime resolution calls peppered through business logic. Remediation strategies include splitting responsibilities, creating small factories for collections of related collaborators, or grouping related parameters into small value objects. Key takeaway: use DI to simplify composition but avoid patterns that obscure dependencies or create God objects. Deciding when to use Dependency Injection comes down to trade-offs. Use DI when a component relies on a collaborator whose behavior may vary by environment, when you need to test behavior without external systems, or when multiple implementations are plausible. For core, always-required collaborators prefer constructor injection because it enforces valid initialization. For optional extensions, use setter injection but validate presence when required. Interface injection is rare; use it only if a framework or legacy pattern demands it. Consider an example given in the chapter: a ReportGenerator that needs different data readers. Constructor injection of an IDataReader is the best option because the report generator cannot function without a data source, making the dependency required for the object's lifetime. Containers become valuable when application composition grows complex and manual wiring becomes a maintenance burden. Key takeaway: match the injection style to the dependency’s role — required, optional, or framework-driven. The composition root is a central place where the application composes its object graph and wires dependencies. Keep composition code separate from business logic: create concrete implementations and pass them into constructors at application startup or in a small composition module. For example, in a console application you might instantiate SqlUserRepository with its connection string, then create a UserService with that repository and pass UserService to the application entry point. In larger apps this logic can be expressed through a container configuration, but the principle remains: keep wiring visible and controlled. Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. First, Inversion of Control is a design principle that separates composition from behavior. Second, Dependency Injection is a practical pattern to implement IoC by providing dependencies from outside the class. Third, constructor injection is the default for required dependencies because it enforces a valid state, while setter and interface injection are options for optional or framework-driven needs. Fourth, IoC containers automate registration and resolution in larger systems but should not hide dependencies. Finally, watch for DI smells such as overly long constructors, service locator usage, and over-injecting trivial objects. Keep composition centralized, prefer simple manual wiring when possible, and introduce containers when complexity warrants it. These ideas work together to produce code that is modular, testable, and easier to evolve. First, decoupling is the practical benefit: DI reduces direct dependencies so you can change implementations and write focused tests. Second, pick the right injection style: constructor for required, setter for optional, and interface injection only when needed by a framework or legacy requirement. Third, use containers judiciously: they automate wiring and lifecycle but should not hide what a component depends on. Keep composition visible in a central composition root, avoid service locators, and refactor classes that take too many dependencies.
